505.title: Living ashtpadi 17
505.hook: truth in Sukhmani is lived, not argued
505.howItsDone: Sikhs often cite Guru Nanak's teaching that truthful living stands above truth itself, and Japji Sahib, recited each morning, opens its first stanza with the question of how to become sachiaar, truthful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, true are His devotees, and your line: become true. Did you keep one small promise, quietly? Today we close the seventeenth ashtpadi by living it. Day five hundred five.

Somewhere online, right now, two people are arguing about what's true. They've been at it for forty replies. Each has links, each has receipts, neither has moved an inch. Meanwhile, somewhere else, a woman is quietly returning a wallet she found, with every bill still inside, and nobody will ever post about it. Which of those two scenes has more truth in it? Most of us know the answer without thinking. Guru Nanak put it into a single line, and it's the key to the seventeenth ashtpadi. Today: truth lived.
screen: `FORTY REPLIES, NOBODY MOVES.` → `A WALLET RETURNED, EVERY BILL.` → `WHICH HAS MORE TRUTH?`

segments.voice: This week the seventeenth ashtpadi gave us three pictures. Truth runs through all time: aad sach. Truth runs through everything: true His feet, true who touches them, the true court. And truth spreads to people: the devotee becomes true by contact. Notice what's missing. There's no argument. No proof. Sukhmani doesn't try to convince anyone that truth exists. It assumes truth, and asks what happens to a life that touches it. Guru Nanak said it outright in Sri Raag, in a line many Sikhs know: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living. Sach aachaar. Aachaar means conduct, the way you behave, how you actually live. So above truth as an idea sits truth as a habit. That's an unusual ranking. Many people think of truth mainly as something to know or defend. Gurbani puts the weight on something to do. It goes all the way back to the beginning of Japji, which you heard at the start of this path. Guru Nanak's very first question there is: kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai? How does one become sachiaar, a truthful one? Not: how do we prove what's true? How do we become it? And the answer Japji gives isn't a debate. It's a way of walking: in the order of the One's will. So living ashtpadi 17 isn't about winning arguments for truth, even good ones. It's about the wallet. The honest timesheet. The apology without excuses. The plain answer when a dodge would be easier. Truth, in Sukhmani, is a thing you do with your hands.
screen: `TIME, EVERYTHING, PEOPLE: THIS WEEK.` · `NO ARGUMENT, NO PROOF.` · `SACH AACHAAR: TRUTHFUL LIVING.` · `KIV SACHIAARAA HOEEAI?` · then, large: `TRUTH LIVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one truth to live today. Not to argue for; to do. Sit and let your day ahead pass in front of you: the meetings, the messages, the errands. Look for one place where a small truth could be done: an honest answer, a fair share, a promise kept, a mistake owned. Choose it. Picture your hands doing it. Then let the plan rest and just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 17. Sach aachaar: truth is high, and higher still is truthful living. Japji's first question asks how to become sachiaar, truthful.
Your line: truth lived. Today, skip one argument about what's true, and do one true thing instead. Day five hundred five.

506.title: Ashtpadi 18, salok: the True Guru
506.hook: the salok honors the True Guru (Sukhmani 18)
506.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the eighteenth ashtpadi with the salok on the True Guru; Sikhs honor God, the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru, and gather as sangat in its presence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 17, and your line: truth lived. Did you do one true thing instead of arguing for one? Today the eighteenth ashtpadi begins, and it's about the one who teaches truth. Day five hundred six.

Think of a teacher who changed something in you. Maybe a third-grade teacher who noticed you were drawing in the margins and gave you a sketchbook. A coach who said one sentence at the right moment. A grandmother who taught you to make bread and, without saying so, taught you patience. Most of us have one or two. Most of us never went back to say thank you. The word Sikh itself is about exactly this relationship. And the salok of the eighteenth ashtpadi is about the teacher at its center. Today: the True Guru.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO CHANGED YOU.` → `A SKETCHBOOK. ONE SENTENCE. BREAD.` → `NEVER WENT BACK TO SAY THANKS.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: the one who knows the True Being is called the True Guru. In his company the Sikh is carried across; Nanak, sing the praises of the Lord. Start with the second word you heard there: Sikh. It comes from a Sanskrit word for a student, a learner, a disciple. A Sikh, at root, is someone who is learning. Not someone who has finished. Which means every Sikh is defined by a relationship: you can't be a learner without a teacher. Then satgur, the True Guru. Notice how the salok defines it. Not by title, not by miracle, not by birth. By knowing: the one who knows the True Being, sat purakh, is the True Guru. Sikhs understand the True Guru in more than one way, and they hold these together. God is the True Guru, the first and final teacher. The ten Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, are honored as the True Guru, one light in ten lives. And since 1708, the Guru Granth Sahib itself, the scripture, is the living Guru, and the community of the Khalsa is called the Guru Panth. When this salok says in his company, Sikhs today hear the sangat gathered around the Guru Granth Sahib. Then the last phrase: sing the praises. The response to having a true teacher isn't to admire the teacher from a distance. It's to sing: to turn the gratitude outward, toward the One the teacher points to. That's the pattern of the next few days. The Guru cares for the Sikh. The Sikh serves. And the line runs both ways.
screen: `SIKH: A LEARNER.` · `SATGUR: THE ONE WHO KNOWS THE TRUE.` · `GOD, TEN GURUS, THE GRANTH.` · `IN HIS COMPANY, SING.` · then, large: `THANK THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teacher. Bring one to mind: a schoolteacher, a mentor, a parent, an author, anyone who taught you something true. See their face, or their handwriting, or the room where you learned from them. Remember one specific thing they gave you. Then thank them, silently, in plain words. If they're still living, notice whether you could send that thank-you for real today. If you pray, thank the One they pointed you toward. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 18. Its salok: the one who knows the True Being is the True Guru, and in that company the Sikh, the learner, is carried across.
Your line: thank the teacher. Today, send one real thank-you to someone who taught you something, and name the thing. Day five hundred six.

507.title: The Guru cherishes the Sikh
507.hook: satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal: the True Guru cherishes and protects the Sikh (Sukhmani 18)
507.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the eighteenth ashtpadi's first stanza on how the True Guru cherishes the Sikh, and many describe feeling that care through the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 18, and your line: thank the teacher. Did a thank-you reach someone who taught you? Today the first stanza turns it around: what the teacher does for the learner. Day five hundred seven.

A kid learning to ride a bike. The parent runs alongside, one hand on the back of the seat, breathing hard. The kid wobbles, yells don't let go, and the parent says I won't. And then, at some point, the parent does let go, and keeps running anyway, a few steps behind, just in case. The kid doesn't even know. They think they're doing it alone. Most of us were held like that at some point, more often than we noticed. The first stanza of the eighteenth ashtpadi is a list of ways the Guru does exactly this for the Sikh. Today: the Guru cherishes the Sikh.
screen: `ONE HAND ON THE SEAT.` → `DON'T LET GO. I WON'T.` → `STILL RUNNING, A FEW STEPS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens: satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal. The True Guru cherishes the Sikh. Pratipaal is a lovely word. It means to nurture, protect, raise up, the way a parent raises a child or a gardener tends a plant. Then the stanza goes line by line, almost like a list of a parent's jobs. In paraphrase: the Guru is always kind to the one who serves. The Guru washes away the dirt of the Sikh's bad thinking. The Guru cuts the Sikh's bonds. The Guru gives the Sikh the wealth of the Name. The Guru sets right the Sikh's life, both this world and the next. And then the last line, the tenderest: Nanak, the True Guru holds the Sikh close, like his own life. Count what's on that list. Cleaning, freeing, giving, arranging, holding. Almost none of it is something the Sikh asked for in the moment. The Guru notices the dirt before the Sikh does. Cuts the bond the Sikh didn't know was there. That's what pratipaal means: care that runs ahead of the request. Notice too that the stanza says this is ongoing. Not a single rescue, but a whole relationship. For Sikhs today, that care is felt through the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat: the hymn that arrives exactly when it's needed, the langar plate handed to you before you knew you were hungry. Many Sikhs would say they've been held like the kid on the bike, far more often than they noticed. That's what today's word asks you to notice. Not to earn. Just to see.
screen: `PRATIPAAL: TO NURTURE AND PROTECT.` · `CLEAN, FREE, GIVE, ARRANGE, HOLD.` · `CARE THAT RUNS AHEAD OF THE ASK.` · `HELD MORE OFTEN THAN WE NOTICE.` · then, large: `CHERISHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel cared for. Sit comfortably and let yourself be supported: by the chair, the floor, the air you're breathing. Then think back to one time you were cared for before you asked: a meal left out for you, a ride offered, a word that came at the right time. Let yourself feel it again, without explaining it away. If you pray, you can feel that care as the Guru's. If not, just let it be care. The bell holds the time.
The Guru cherishes the Sikh. Satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal: care that cleans, frees, gives and holds the Sikh close, like the Guru's own life.
screen: `THE GURU CHERISHES THE SIKH — today's word`.

508.title: The Sikh's service
508.hook: the Sikh serves, and the Guru's teaching fills the Sikh (Sukhmani 18)
508.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara, cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning and minding shoes, usually unpaid and unasked; Sukhmani's eighteenth ashtpadi describes service without desire for reward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Guru cherishes the Sikh, and your line: cherished. Did you notice care that came before you asked? Today, the second stanza turns to what the Sikh does in return. Day five hundred eight.

Walk into the langar hall of a big gurdwara at lunchtime and look past the food. Someone is rolling rotis by the hundred. Someone is stirring a pot of dal the size of a bathtub. A teenager is collecting empty plates. An older man is wiping the floor. In the shoe room by the door, someone you'll never see again is handing back your shoes, polished. Almost none of them are paid. Almost none of them were asked. Ask them why, and many will say some version of: it fills me up. Today: the Sikh's service.
screen: `ROTIS BY THE HUNDRED.` → `YOUR SHOES, HANDED BACK POLISHED.` → `IT FILLS ME UP.`

segments.voice: The second stanza of the eighteenth ashtpadi describes the Sikh who lives in the Guru's house. In paraphrase: the servant who stays in the Guru's home accepts the Guru's command in his heart. He doesn't make a show of himself. He keeps the Name in his heart, and sells his mind to the True Guru. And then the line the whole stanza turns on: one who serves without desire for reward attains the Lord. The word is nihkaamee. Nih, without; kaam, desire, wanting. Serving without wanting something back. Not even thanks. Not even the good feeling of being seen serving. That's why the stanza also says he doesn't make a show of himself. Seva that's done for the photo isn't quite seva yet. Now here's the surprising part, and it's the reason for today's line. You'd think serving without wanting anything would leave you empty. You gave and got nothing. But the stanza says the opposite: the one who serves this way receives the Lord, the very thing every other kind of getting was hoping for. Yesterday the Guru filled the Sikh with the wealth of the Name. Today, the Sikh's service turns out to be the open hand that wealth falls into. That's what the people in the langar mean when they say it fills them up. They didn't serve in order to be filled; then it wouldn't be nihkaamee. They served, and found themselves filled. Sikh history is full of this. Guru Amar Das carrying water, Bhai Lehna carrying wet grass for Guru Nanak. Service first; filling follows.
screen: `LIVING IN THE GURU'S HOUSE.` · `NO SHOW OF HIMSELF.` · `NIHKAAMEE: WITHOUT WANTING.` · `THE OPEN HAND IS FILLED.` · then, large: `SERVE AND BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one unasked service. Sit and picture the people around you today: at home, at work, on your street. Look for one small need nobody has asked you to meet. A full trash can. A coworker's empty mug. A neighbor's recycling bin left at the curb. Choose one. Picture doing it without being seen, and without needing to be. Then let the plan rest, and just breathe. The bell holds the time.
The Sikh's service. Nihkaamee seva: service without wanting, no show, no reward, and the stanza says it is exactly what gets filled.
Your line: serve and be filled. Do one helpful thing today that nobody asked for, and don't mention it to anyone. Day five hundred eight.

509.title: Living ashtpadi 18
509.hook: the bond of Guru and Sikh runs both ways
509.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Vaisakhi 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh initiated the Panj Pyare and then received amrit from them, and many sing aape gur chela; the eighteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani describes the Guru's care and the Sikh's service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sikh's service, and your line: serve and be filled. Did you do one unasked thing, and keep quiet about it? Today we close the eighteenth ashtpadi with a famous day in 1699. Day five hundred nine.
screen: `THE SIKH'S SERVICE — SERVE AND BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Anandpur, at the spring festival of Vaisakhi, 1699, as Sikh tradition tells it. A huge crowd. Guru Gobind Singh stands before them with a drawn sword and asks for a head. Silence. Then one man stands up. Then another, and another, until five have come forward. The Guru initiates them with amrit, sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, and names them the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. Everyone expects that to be the climax. It isn't. What the Guru does next is the part Sikhs still sing about. Today: both ways.
screen: `VAISAKHI, 1699.` → `FIVE COME FORWARD.` → `WHAT THE GURU DOES NEXT.`

segments.voice: Having initiated the five, the Guru kneels before them and asks them to initiate him in the same way. The teacher takes amrit from his own students. A later poet, writing in the tradition of Bhai Gurdas, put it in a line Sikhs still sing: wonderful is Gobind Singh, himself the Guru and himself the disciple. Aape gur chela. That moment is the eighteenth ashtpadi, lived out. This week the ashtpadi showed us two directions. First, the Guru toward the Sikh: the True Guru cherishes, cleans, frees and holds the Sikh close, like his own life. Then the Sikh toward the Guru: living in the Guru's house, serving without wanting, making no show. Read separately, those could sound like a ladder: the Guru on top, giving; the Sikh below, serving. But at Anandpur the ladder becomes a circle. The Guru serves the Sikhs; the Sikhs become a kind of Guru; the Khalsa, the community, is later called the Guru Panth. Care goes down, service goes up, and then they trade places. That's what both ways means. It's also why, for many Sikhs, the relationship isn't one of fear. A Sikh keeps the daily banis, the five articles of faith, the honest work, not as payment to a distant master but as their half of a bond in which the other half is already given. The Guru keeps faith with the Sikh. The Sikh keeps faith with the Guru. Neither half works alone. And on an ordinary day, that bond lives in very small things: one hymn read, one practice kept, one promise to the Guru not quietly dropped.
screen: `THE GURU KNEELS TO THE FIVE.` · `AAPE GUR CHELA.` · `A LADDER BECOMES A CIRCLE.` · `TWO HALVES OF ONE BOND.` · then, large: `BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one practice to keep for the Guru, or for whatever teacher or path you're walking. It can be very small: these few minutes every day; one line of a hymn each morning; a single act of honest work done carefully. Sit and decide on it. Then rest in the other half of the bond: the care that's already been given to you, whether you noticed it or not. Hold both halves together. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 18. Aape gur chela: at Anandpur the Guru became the disciple of his own disciples. Care and service, running both ways.
Your line: both ways. Today, keep the one practice you chose, and remember it's your half of a bond, not a payment. Day five hundred nine.

510.title: Ashtpadi 19, salok: nothing goes along
510.hook: nothing goes with you except devotion (Sukhmani 19)
510.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the nineteenth ashtpadi with the salok saath na chaalai bin bhajan, and Sikh life pairs honest earning with remembering the Name as the wealth that lasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 18, and your line: both ways. Did you keep the one practice you chose? Today Sukhmani enters its last stretch, ashtpadis nineteen to twenty-four, and the nineteenth begins with a hard look at what we own. Day five hundred ten.

Anyone who has cleared out a parent's home knows the feeling. The drawers of rubber bands. The good china used twice. The boxes of papers that once mattered terribly: tax forms, warranties, letters. A lifetime of things, and all of it, every last bit, stayed behind. You stand in the half-empty room holding a coffee mug and realize the person isn't in any of it. The salok of the nineteenth ashtpadi says this out loud, and then says what isn't left behind. Today: nothing goes along.
screen: `CLEARING OUT A PARENT'S HOME.` → `A LIFETIME OF THINGS, ALL LEFT.` → `THE PERSON ISN'T IN ANY OF IT.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: nothing goes along with you except devotion; all the poison of worldly things is ash. Earn the Name of the Lord; Nanak, this is the excellent wealth. Three words open it. Saath: with, alongside, company. Na chaalai: does not go. Bin bhajan: except devotion, the singing and remembering of God. So the first line is a short inventory. Everything you own, check the list, and next to almost every item: does not go. Then the strong image: bikhiaa saglee chhaar. Bikhiaa is a word Gurbani uses for maya's poison, the pull of worldly things. Chhaar is ash. Not evil, exactly. Ash: what's left when the fire has burned out. The house, the car, the savings account aren't wicked. They're just ash-in-waiting. Then the turn, and it's a money word. Kamaavanaa: to earn. Earn the Name. The salok doesn't tell you to stop earning; Sikhs are expected to work honestly and provide for their families. It tells you what else to earn. And it calls the Name dhan, wealth, and saar, the excellent, the essential. So this isn't a hymn against wealth. It's a hymn about which wealth travels. Over the next days the ashtpadi will look at what stays behind and what does go along. Today, only the inventory. And notice that the salok makes no threat. It simply points at the room full of things and says: none of this comes with you, except the devotion.
screen: `SAATH NA CHAALAI: DOES NOT GO ALONG.` · `BIKHIAA IS ASH: CHHAAR.` · `KAMAAVANAA: EARN THE NAME.` · `WHICH WEALTH TRAVELS?` · then, large: `NOTHING GOES ALONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your possessions. Let your eyes move slowly around the room you're in: the furniture, the phone, the clothes, the books, the screen. To each thing, without judging it, say silently: this stays. Not with sadness; just accurately. Then, at the end, close your eyes and ask: what, if anything, is going along with me? Let the question sit without answering it. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 19. Its salok: saath na chaalai bin bhajan. Nothing goes along except devotion; earn the Name, the excellent wealth.
Your line: nothing goes along. Today, before you buy something, pause and say silently: this stays. Then decide. Day five hundred ten.

511.title: Wealth stays behind
511.hook: riches, youth and power are left behind (Sukhmani 19)
511.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the janamsakhi story of Duni Chand and the needle, and many practice dasvandh, giving a tenth of their earnings; Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi names riches, youth and power as things left behind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 19, and your line: nothing goes along. Did you pause before buying something? It's the end of a week: truth lived, thank the teacher, cherished, serve and be filled, both ways, nothing goes along. Today, a story with a needle in it. Day five hundred eleven.

Sikhs tell a story about a rich man in Lahore named Duni Chand. He was so wealthy that he flew flags over his house, one for every large sum he owned. When Guru Nanak came through the city, Duni Chand invited him to a grand meal and asked if there was anything he could do for him. Guru Nanak took out a small sewing needle and handed it to him. Keep this for me, he said, and give it back to me in the next world. Duni Chand happily agreed. Then he went home, looked at the needle, and couldn't sleep.
screen: `A RICH MAN WITH FLAGS.` → `KEEP THIS NEEDLE FOR ME.` → `GIVE IT BACK IN THE NEXT WORLD.`

segments.voice: In the story, Duni Chand's wife asks him what's wrong, and he shows her the needle. She asks the obvious question: how exactly are you going to carry a needle into the next world? He goes back to Guru Nanak. I can't take this with me. And Guru Nanak answers: if you can't take a needle, how will you take all those flags? It's a janamsakhi story, from the old tellings of Guru Nanak's life, and like many of them it's a picture, not a court record. But it says in one small object what the nineteenth ashtpadi says in its stanzas. Riches stay behind. So do youth, beauty and power. Gurbani returns to this constantly: the body we're proud of, the house we built, the position we fought for, none of it comes along. Notice the needle, though. It isn't a big thing. It's the smallest, lightest, most portable thing Guru Nanak could find. If even that stays, everything stays. The story is gentle with Duni Chand. Nobody shames him. The tradition says he took the lesson and began giving his wealth to feed people. And that's the practical turn Sikhs take from this. If wealth stays behind anyway, the question becomes what you do with it while you hold it. Sikh tradition encourages dasvandh, giving a tenth of what you earn, and the langar exists because people give. Giving something away isn't losing it. It was always going to be left behind. Giving it just chooses where it lands.
screen: `HOW WILL YOU CARRY A NEEDLE?` · `A PICTURE, NOT A COURT RECORD.` · `RICHES, YOUTH, POWER: ALL STAY.` · `DASVANDH: CHOOSE WHERE IT LANDS.` · then, large: `LEFT BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one thing to give away. Picture the things you own, and let one rise up: a coat you don't wear, a book you've finished, a tool someone else could use, some money you could spare. Don't pick the hardest thing; pick one real thing. Picture it in someone else's hands, being used. Notice how that feels. Then decide when you'll give it. The bell holds the time.
Wealth stays behind. Riches, youth and power, even a needle: none of it comes along, so the question is where you let it land.
Your line: left behind. Give one thing away today, an object or some money, to someone who will use it. Day five hundred eleven.
